subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin this debate by indicating my appreciation to members of this subcommittee.

February 26, 1993
Routine Proceedings
I would like to compliment the chairman of the committee, the member for South Shore, the member for Drummond who spent many hours working, and the member for Victoria. I would like to compliment the hon. member for Don Valley West, the member for Northumberland and the member for Cambridge.
I say that because in my 14 years of experience in the House this committee was one of the most important inquiries undertaken by a Commons committee. It did not receive a great deal of publicity but it delved into issues that go to the very heart of the significant changes taking place in the world around us and the impact that those changes have in our own country.
It opened up for many of us a look at the arcane, confusing and dangerous world of the international arms trade and Canada's role in that precarious business. It made us look very seriously at the question of the defence industries in Canada and what was happening to them. It made us look at how they are being affected by the substantial shift in procurement policies and the whole nature of the development of high technology that was so much part of the defence weapons systems during the cold war. They are now being substantially altered and affected by a major shift toward a peacemaking capacity for Canada.
It made us come to grips with some very tough choices as Canadians. I do not in any way underplay the incredible, tough, realistic problems that are faced by many communities, businesses and Canadians in making decisions about whether we continue as we have been doing. We are a reasonably significant player in the production of arms in this country.
Can we make a turn in the road toward a different attitude, a different approach occasioned by the demands of the post cold war world?
Perhaps the importance of the work of the committee has been highlighted in the way that the estimates that were tabled in the House of Commons displayed a certain set of choices.
On one hand we know there are significant cutbacks for economic development for native people, promotion of cultural activities in this country, young people in education and training, health care and seniors. There is a whole list of Canadians who are being asked to sacrifice on the basis of restrained budgets and limited resources.
On the other side of the ledger there is an increase of $1.4 billion to a helicopter project of $4.4 billion, bringing the total to $5.8 billion for a weapons system that is becoming increasingly irrelevant in terms of the changes going on in the world around us.
At some time there may have been justification for the submarine detecting helicopters it bought in terms of our cold war responsibilities as a member of the NATO alliance.
Surely in today's world when the submarine threat is no longer there and the Russians have downed tools in large part, for us to proceed with a massive expenditure of $5.8 billion while at the same time making substantial cuts across the board in a whole range of industrial, economic and social programs just shows how crucial it is that this country get its mind around, and get a grip on, the real priorities in Canada.
That is what this committee tried to do. It tried to understand that the weapons trade is not in the best interest of Canada. One of the most tragic sets of figures and facts presented to members of the committee showed how in so many parts of the world the billions upon billions of dollars being spent on arms work to victimize women, children and people who no longer have the means of the basic essentials of life.
Somalia is a good example. We are now mounting massive efforts in Somalia through the UN not only to keep the peace but to rebuild the society. In the 10 or so years up to the outbreak of the civil war a billion dollars worth of arms was poured into Somalia by the Americans, the Russians and others. Now the UN and Canadian troops are having to contend with those arms. There are enough weapons in Somalia to keep that conflict going for 100 years.
Now we are paying an enormous price for it in trying to keep the peace because of this vast haemorrhaging of arms exports.
During the gulf war one of the great declarations made by the Prime Minister and others was that we were fighting the war to secure the peace in the Middle East. One of the objectives was to suffocate the arms race in the Middle East and to suppress the vast amounts of money that went into places like Iraq with which we have to contend afterwards.
February 26, 1993

What has happened since then? One report I read recently said that in Iran alone over $100 billion is being spent on new arms. The United States of America has just finished in the last fiscal year exporting close to $6 billion worth of arms into parts of the Middle East. Regretfully and sadly, our own country is also becoming an arms supplier in this most volatile of areas.
It would be a foolhardy person not to know that some day those arms may come back to haunt us. We will be paying a much larger price in terms of the blood of young men and women because of the need to make a profit.
In southeast Asia last year alone close to $90 billion was spent on arms. That takes away money that would be much better used for the development of the human potential in these areas.
One of the sadnesses we have is the need for all of us to see how we can provide some leadership. My colleague from Nepean points out another very important and salient fact. The United States of America spent $1 million a day in El Salvador. Now the amount of money the international community has to put in for peacekeeping efforts must try to contend with that incredible arsenal which was built up over the years.
This committee tried to come to grips with that issue by saying that we know that Canada alone cannot do the job. We must do a better job than we are doing to give a message to the world that the proliferation of arms must come to a halt. That is the reason for the recommendation to have a much tougher munitions control register. It was designed to say that we would not be party to sending arms to any area, region or country in which there are human rights abuses, civil conflict, or dictatorships using those arms to suppress people or create violence or conflict.
It is a message and a signal to other countries to hopefully follow the lead. It does not mean to say that arms exports are prohibited because we recognize the reality that we do have allies and friends that we have some mutual interest in supporting, such as NATO, the United States and some other places.
We want to make sure there is a system in which there could be a clear requirement that exports would only go
Routine Proceedings
to countries on the list and that there would be a transparency to that list so we would know who they are. We want to make sure that it would not be decided inside the bowels of External Affairs and all of a sudden an announcement would be made and before anything could be done it would be over, as happened with the sale of light armoured vehicles to Saudi Arabia.
Furthermore, and it is a very important principle, we felt it crucial that Parliament have a role and that the elected representatives of the people of Canada should be given some opportunity to determine whether we want to sell arms to country A or country B. Therefore there is a requirement for tabling the name of any country that would go on this list to be reviewed by Parliament if we so decided.
We also understood that once that was done the system should be reasonably efficient in its processing. There is no reason to hold up companies unduly. Once the country was on the list then the processing could take place with some degree of effectiveness. The point of the matter is that we believed it was time for Canada to take some leadership.
We also recognized at the same time that it is not simply enough to put a prohibition or a limitation on the sale of arms. We have to look at the much broader and more critical substantial issue of how to convert those defence industries that have been creating arms to effective peacetime uses. This is a very important issue that is being faced by all countries.
It was interesting to see that in the campaign statements of President Clinton he talked about how to begin to transfer the enormous research and development capacity of the defence establishment into an effective reallocation to peacetime uses.
Our committee concluded exactly the same thing. It is important for Canada to begin to do the kind of analysis and reconstruction of its own policies to support and facilitate the conversion of our defence industries.
We came to that conclusion for a couple of very good reasons. First, our defence industries contain some of the best high technology minds in the country. It is on the high technology end that we have been providing parts and components over the years and we do not want to lose those skills.

February 26, 1993
Routine Proceedings
Surely we should have learned from the example of the Avro Arrow that those people working in those industries have incredibly good skills that could be used for other purposes.
Let me give one very good example. We all recognize, at least on this side of the House, that the whole issue of peacemaking is becoming central to our security. The contribution to and involvement in international collective security initiatives, whether in Bosnia, Somalia, Cambodia or wherever, is really the security issue of the future.
We believe we have to shift our spending priorities in the defence department to meet those requirements so that Canada can fulfil its role as a peacemaker. It is totally ridiculous and unacceptable for the Minister of National Defence to keep standing up in this House to say we have to begin pulling back our commitments on peacekeeping because we do not have enough money to get enough troops and to train and equip them properly.
At the same time she condoned, supported and endorsed an expenditure of $5.8 billion for helicopters which have no use in peacemaking. It is an absolutely and totally ridiculous contradiction in terms.
We should understand the time has come for Canadians and the Canadian government to make tough choices as recommended in this committee. It is time to shift our priorities and understand that the world has changed. We cannot have a Minister of National Defence walking around in a fog buying into the old cold war strategies and stratagems. That simply does not do any good for our international reputation and what we can do in our own country.
One of the opportunities this new peacekeeping role represents is the need for new kinds of technology for verification, observation and monitoring to make sure that arms are not spread into countries and we can monitor what happens to nuclear plants in Iraq if need be. There is an incredible need at the United Nations level and other areas for a much more sophisticated international monitoring observation system. We are well equipped to begin making contributions in those areas, to help our industries develop a capacity to meet
the world-wide need for those peacemaking technologies.
That is what the report talks about. It was a very important insight for us to see many of the plants. Our engineers and skilled technicians are anxious to get into those areas but unfortunately the fix of government policies in a sense almost prohibits it because we are not interested in supporting that. There is no conversion plan for Canada. The DIPP funds are not designed for conversion. They are designed to keep doing the same old thing.

speechtext:
I am going to come to that in just a moment. In the second dimension, the onus is not simply on the shift of military priorities to peacemaking. There is also an incredible opportunity to use technologies presently located in our defence industries for a wide variety of civilian uses.
My friend from Broadview-Greenwood points out the incredible demand for new environmental technology. We met with officials of a company in western Canada that is now beginning to develop a technique for sensoring using technology which has been used for spy satellites. It will now begin to focus on how many fish there are in the North Pacific or what is happening to the glaciers in the north or what is happening to the atmosphere. It will use its sensoring techniques to detect the environmental changes occurring around the world. It is an incredible growth market. When asked to what extent the company can be assisted and helped in making that conversion, there is none. It is not there. It simply does not exist.
One of the most important and significant proposals contained in this committee report is that the question of conversion be made a priority for our government. The government should table a plan and restructure the DIPP program to encourage conversion techniques. It should establish a centre to help industries plan and develop to adapt to peacetime uses.
It is an incredible opportunity to reconstruct our industrial strength in this country. We can use our best minds and skills not in the production of weapons but in the production of new high technology jobs and products that the world is going to need.
February 26, 1993

This report should not go on the shelf. It needs to be read by every member of this House. It should be read certainly by government officials and ministers responsible. Certainly I recommend that the Minister of National Defence read it, if she is not too busy.
Maybe she would come to some understanding of the serious mistake she is making in not doing a significant reassessment, review and reallocation of the priorities within that department. Then we can begin moving into areas that would give Canada some real leadership and some real opportunities internationally to try to suppress the developments in the arms race. At the same time and in the same way we can come to grips with the need to change our own priorities at home and to begin to stimulate, encourage and facilitate a shift and change in our defence industries to meet peacetime peacemaking uses.
It was a great privilege being a member of that committee. The document itself will serve in the future as part of a blueprint. It is not complete, committees cannot do that. It sets the direction, it sets a way. It tries to break out of the old thinking and tries to look ahead. For that reason I strongly recommend that members of this House endorse and support this report and particularly that members of the government read it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was not sure if we were going to have a period for questions or not, but I will commence my debate.
I was a member of that subcommittee. Indeed, it was a wonderful opportunity for myself, for my colleague from Drummond and for other members of the committee to look at this matter and put forward the report, Future of Canadian Military Goods Production and Export.
I want to take a few moments to put on the record some comments on the existing Canadian export control system which I believe is one of the strictest in the world. That is what the debate wrapped around. Canada as a nation probably has one of the strictest export control regimes in the world. I think that has to be understood.
The question is how to improve or why change something that is the strictest? It is important that
Routine Proceedings
people understand that export control permits just do not relate to guns. They relate to a wide range of items.
Canada has consistently advocated arrangements at the international level. These have been aimed at building security frameworks that effectively take account of both the military and non-military threats to security, that promote habits of dialogue and co-operation and that emphasize conflict prevention rather than conflict resolution by force.
Unfortunately, despite the great progress in the security and arms control field in recent years, we have not yet achieved the degree of success Canada wants and needs. For the foreseeable future Canada and other countries will still have to maintain a reasonable level of armed forces to deter, and if necessary, to respond to military threats to security and to participate in collective security and peacekeeping operations.
The need for countries to maintain reasonable levels of armed forces was fully recognized in the arms control initiative announced by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in February 1991. This initiative called for efforts to prevent excessive buildup of conventional arms. By excessive buildup of conventional arms Canada means a buildup that goes beyond reasonable defence requirements. Canada is not proposing to stop exporting and importing military goods, nor is it telling other countries to stop doing so.
At the global level Canada was a leading participant in the negotiations in the UN leading to the establishment of a global conventional arms register. Canada must now work to ensure effective implementation of that register and will seek to build on it with the view of increasing the scope of its coverage and providing further avenues of consultation.
At the national level Canada has for the past three years issued an annual report on the export of military goods from Canada. I know that the member from Winnipeg mentioned Somalia, Iran, El Salvador. If Canadians looked at the report that is issued annually, Canada has not sent $1 worth of items under the export control list to those three countries. I think he did acknowledge that Canada is not participating.

February 26, 1993
Routine Proceedings
The matter they want to deal with is: "We have to take this export control list and apply it to countries rather than the process of each individual application being looked at".
What I would like to do now is read some comments I had put into the particular report. Again, I mention that the existing export control permit system is one of the strictest in the world. I will read directly from the report: "One committee member", which is myself, "strongly believes that the recommendations relating to establishing a munitions country control list will produce undesirable results".
I argued that to merge the items on the export control list group two with the rules to establish a country on the automatic firearms country control list would not produce a stable and transparent public policy environment and would place Canadian business at a competitive disadvantage.
The proposed munitions country control list would initially consist of only 10 countries, since only Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States have concluded intergovernmental defence research, development and production arrangements with Canada.
I want to digress for a moment. If we want to send firearms to a country we have to go through a lot of work in the development of arrangements. This is very difficult to do, and Canada has only set up 10 such arrangements with 10 countries.
The proposed munitions country control list process would establish a process that tells Canadian companies that they can expect a permit to be issued without delay to allow them to sell bombs, torpedoes, rockets and missiles to Denmark but they could be denied permission to sell transport aircraft spare parts to Kenya. For example, this could have meant that in 1990 exports to Brazil of underwater detection devices, to India of electronic generators, to Kuwait of bomb disposal suits, to Morocco of aircraft flight simulators and to Singapore of fire control systems would not have been possible.
Rather than the current system of examining each application on its own individual unique merit their suggestion is that once a country is approved then anything can be sent to that country. That is important to
understand because this would have meant that in 1991 exports of military goods or components that come under the Export Control Act, and that includes things such as fire control systems and bomb disposal suits, to countries such as Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, which represents about 30 per cent of the controlled Canadian sales, would not have been permitted.
As a result of this recommendation we would say to Australians: "You are not on this list and therefore we do not trust you". That is the impact of the recommendations that they are making.
I further argued that this formula process could not be used as each case must consider the present climate in the country of destination, the goods to be exported and the potential end use. The current export control system already addresses every application as having a possible unique circumstance.
Canada can take a lead at the world level, and it already has in the UN, but part of the recommendations in this report basically say to the Canadian industries involved in this area: "We do not want you to do any business. We want you to go out of business", because that is the stranglehold that they would put on these businesses.
There is also the question about whether we should help these companies to convert. I can assure the House, based on the witnesses who have come forward, that companies already recognize that the cold war is over and that countries are not buying the amount of military goods they used to buy. It is a changing world and the businesses in that industry recognized that many years ago. They have already started their own conversion programs.
Therefore this is best left to those sectors that are motivated by profit because they recognize that they are in a shrinking market and that they must diversify and use the skills and technologies they have. A lot of the products they make do have dual purpose uses.
I think industry has already recognized that. If industry is sitting back waiting for the government to put together a committee to go out and tell all these companies how they should convert then those companies will not survive. Those companies have already started to do that.

February 26, 1993

There are many things in this report that I like and I support. However, I do not agree with the recommendation to change the export control permit. It already issues reports, is very transparent and is considered to be one of the strictest in the world. I do not believe there is any evidence to indicate we should change it.
I could continue but I know that my colleague from Victoria certainly has his point of view. He expressed it in committee and I know he will do so on the floor of the House. I will now yield to him.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to support the motion that this House concur in the recommendations of this committee's report. The committee worked very hard to produce a constructive and useful report on this important issue and I think the recommendations are to be commended to the House.
Let me recall how this subcommittee came about. At the time of the gulf war the world became aware of the fact that the arms trade, which in the first sentence of this report is called a monument to cold war international relations, had turned the arms production industry which grew out of World War II into an export trade to developing countries. By 1977, 80 per cent of the world's production was drifting into developing countries. We saw the folly of that in the gulf war. There was a brief moment when it appeared that the world might be resolved to try to deal with that issue, to try to bring the arms export industry around the world, and the scandal of the arms sales, under control.
Our Prime Minister made a very eloquent speech during the gulf war calling on the United Nations to convene a world summit to deal with arms exports. However within weeks of the end of the cold war the government seemed to have forgotten the eloquent statements and brought before this House Bill C-6 which authorized the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia, contrary to previous government policy.
In the course of that debate the government conceded that the issue needed to be examined by Parliament. I was very pleased that the Minister for International Trade accepted my proposal that a subcommittee be established through the committee on external affairs.
In the summer and fall of 1991 the committee began its work. We travelled across Canada and heard repre-
Routine Proceedings
sentations from people throughout this country, from Victoria, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Halifax, Montreal and Ottawa. We also heard from experts and government officials. I believe that we have put together in this report a very useful examination of how the world got into this mess and of Canada's contribution to it.
It should be understood that Canada is the eighth largest producer of arms on the globe. It is the 14th largest exporter of arms in the world. We contribute to the problem and we have a responsibility to respond.
The committee report could be divided into a number of sections.
First, we emphasize the importance of Canada using its diplomatic energies in multilateral efforts to bring the arms export industry around the world under control. It is not good enough for Canada to get its own act together. We have to work with other countries, most particularly with the industrial countries, to come up with enforceable common policies to reduce and control the export of arms.
We also have to work with the developing countries to produce secure regimes. Many developing countries are forced by the arms sales to their neighbours to respond in kind. Others are attracted to arms as a means of keeping their own governments in power. That is one of our concerns about sales to Saudi Arabia.
We have to work with other countries to try to produce a secure international order. That must be at the heart of our work in this area. Without that any efforts we make in this country will come to nought.
However, we have a special obligation to get our own act together, particularly if we are going to push other countries in this direction. The committee report outlines some very specific recommendations to make that happen.
We recognize in the report that there may be legitimate reasons for Canada to produce arms. We may need to supply our own police and armed services. The United Nations peacekeeping efforts will require arms. Under appropriate circumstances there are legitimate requirements for military arms to deal with those who would break international law.

February 26, 1993
Routine Proceedings
Therefore it becomes important that we establish an effective arms export regime. This committee report takes the current regime, which is totally internal to the government, and changes it into a statutory regime accountable to Parliament.
As things now stand the government has its own policy and whenever it wishes to make an exception it can do so. The only reason there was Bill C-6 was that because of a particular provision in the Criminal Code in respect of small arms the government was forced to come to Parliament to get a change. But for that the government would simply have changed its policy internally, without any accounting to Parliament at all. It is very important that the arms export system be established by Parliament and be accountable to Parliament.
The system should have two key elements to it. First, there should be a listing of countries to whom arms exports would be acceptable. All other countries would be outside the purview of the export system and exports to those countries would be illegal. If there was an interest in exporting to a country not on the list the government would have to come to Parliament and have the list amended. Second, each transaction would have to be reviewed and, in my view at least, subject to a parliamentary review.
The second element of the policy outlined by the committee is the conversion and diversification of the arms industry. As long as an arms industry exists there will be pressure, as we saw in Bill C-6, on governments and on Parliament to approve exports in the interest of maintaining employment.
Therefore for that reason alone it is very important that we begin to change the industrial structure of this country. In the period after the Second World War, and in particular after the cancellation of the Avro Arrow, the Liberal government of the day embarked on a policy of encouraging the Canadian defence production industry through subsidies and other programs.
So an industry has developed in response to government encouragement, yet it must now face the economic reality that not only are defence budgets beginning to decrease around the world but that the public is calling on governments to control and reduce defence production.
It is a bad, declining, and difficult industry to be in. Therefore from a strictly economic and social point of view it is important that the government encourage a change to civilian and other uses.
It is also important if we are to ensure the maintenance of an effective arms export regime that is not subject to pressure every time a company needs new markets.
We see now today a government which seems determined to ignore the wisdom of this parliamentary committee report. We still have not had a reply from the government. It carries on its policies as if this report did not exist, which is probably not a new phenomenon but continues to be a matter of disappointment. I wonder if the Minister of National Defence or the Secretary of State for External Affairs have even read the report.
It would be very interesting to hear the views on this from the government itself because what happens is that the government gets advice from the bureaucrats who are administering the policy the way they would like to. It seems to me that the government should be ready to rely on the wisdom of a parliamentary committee report and on the wisdom of Parliament. After all this subcommittee went out to the general public in this country to develop a balanced policy that respects the interests of all who are involved, that fits within the over-all policy of this country, and that the public insists upon.
We now see the phenomenon of the government encouraging more sales to countries in the Middle East despite the government's statement that arms exports should not go to areas of potential hostilities. Next week in Ottawa the government is convening a session with its trade commissioners inviting the world to come to Ottawa to look at our arms exports and our capacity to export. What countries are invited? They include Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Iran.
The high tech conference that is scheduled for next week is in direct contravention of the will of the Canadian people as we heard it during the work of this committee and it runs completely counter to the government's own stated policy.
Let me conclude by congratulating the member who introduced this motion. He is the official spokesperson for the Liberal Party on this issue and I am pleased to hear that in that capacity he is endorsing this report. I would hope other members of his party would be equally enthusiastic.
February 26, 1993

During the travels of the committee across the country there was the phenomenon of there frequently being two Liberal representatives. When those who favoured a restrictive policy were appearing before the committee the official spokesperson for the Liberal Party was there and was very supportive of their briefs. When the industry was appearing another member from the Liberal Party would be there and would be falling all over the industry representatives and saying how encouraging the Liberal Party would be to arms exports around the world and to defence production.
There were two voices from the Liberal Party. It would be very encouraging if we could believe that the member from Winnipeg actually represented the view of his party. During debate on Bill C-6 the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace took leadership on that issue. However, I fear that they represent a faint voice within their caucus.
I am looking forward to hearing their leader over the next few months stake his colours as firmly to the mast-head as the member for Winnipeg South Centre has in this debate.
It is crucially important to world order that the countries of the globe come to grips with this issue, and we have a chance now with the end of the cold war. The countries in eastern and central Europe that have themselves depended so much on military production will be looking to the western world to change its ways.
This report offers a guideline to do that. I call on this House to accept the report.

Madam Speaker, dairy producers in the Abitibi region object to Treasury Board's 10 per cent cut in subsidies for dairy products.
I think we should consider the consumer subsidy aspect. According to the arrangement between the Government of Canada, through Agriculture Canada, and Canada's dairy producers, the subsidy enables them to lower their selling price to the industry, which in turn reduces its price to the consumer by the same amount.
We realize that something has to be done about the financial situation of the Canadian Treasury. In fact, that is the purpose of most of the recommendations in the Auditor General's report. The Minister of Finance would be well advised to look at these recommendations and adopt a strategy for their implementation.
According to Rosaire Mongrain, president of the Abitibi dairy producers, their net income will be cut by 10 per cent.

Madam Speaker, the Metropolitan Tbronto Hockey League, under the leadership of John Gardiner, has plans to build an international hockey and figure skating facility on 12 acres of land at the Downsview Air Force Base in Toronto.
This world-class facility will create instant construction jobs, long-term jobs in tourism, longer term jobs in fitness and amateur sport, not to mention the benefit to tens of thousands of figure skaters and hockey players, as well as a home for other Canadian cultural events.
The MTHL has raised the construction money from private sponsors and the government has declared the land redundant.
On behalf of all members of the greater Toronto Liberal caucus we urge this government to cut through the red tape and get this project going. It should remember its promise of jobs, jobs, jobs.

Madam Speaker, speaking on my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Temiscamingue, I want to thank the Prime Minister of Canada for the energy and determination with which he served this country during the past eight years.
The people in my riding have always seen him as a true leader, whose tenacity, determination and courage are extraordinary. We will remember him as a man driven by a consuming passion for his country and as a man of great warmth and generosity who was sensitive and attuned to the needs of the regions.
Clean air, decentralization of federal services, regional development and a Ministry of State for Seniors are all initiatives that were welcomed by my constituents.
I therefore want to join my fellow citizens in wishing the Prime Minister and his family a happy and prosperous retirement, and once again, we want to say, loud and clear: Thank you!

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Madam Speaker, inshore fishermen in the Gulf of St. Lawrence can be accused of feeling that this government and particularly this department of fisheries have it in for them. First it was the imposition of dockside monitoring fees which these fishermen have had to fight in court. Then it was the attack on the bona fide licensing program. Now there is the standoff at the government wharf at Lismore right in the backyard of the Minister of Public Works.
February 26, 1993

It is true the federal government is making much needed repairs to the government wharf. Unfortunately this has required the destruction of a shed owned by a small lobster buyer. The fishermen believe a modest payment to the buyer to help replace this facility is warranted. The amount is negotiable.
Instead, the government wants to provoke a costly court battle with the fishermen, a battle neither it nor the taxpayers of Canada can afford.
Why does this government not try accommodation instead of confrontation in dealing with its inshore fishermen whose backs are against the wall because of its disastrous policies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we were all saddened today to hear of the passing of a great Canadian, Mr. Danny Gallivan.
All Canadians from coast to coast have lost an irreplaceable citizen and a friend. Danny Gallivan will best be remembered as a pioneer. He revolutionized sports broadcasting as we know it today. We will all remember the voice behind Hockey Night in Canada and the Montreal Canadiens. We will surely remember the excitement and the euphoria he brought to our living-rooms on Saturday nights. The scintillating saves and the cannonading drives were all synonymous with Danny Gallivan.
One could feel his love for the game but, more important, his love for his country. Although best remembered as an avid broadcaster, Danny Gallivan nonetheless contributed as much time and dedication to the greatest of his concerns, human welfare.
In fact his love for this country and its people may be best exemplified by the multitude of charitable organizations he supported and contributed to. As well, his love for the youth of Canada was unmatched.
We will all miss Danny Gallivan.

Madam Speaker, the Gwa'Sala and Nakwaxda'xw Indian
bands at Smith Inlet and Blunden Harbour were forcibly amalgamated and moved to Port Hardy, B.C. in the 1960s.
This forcible amalgamation and relocation were exclusively for the convenience of the department of Indian affairs. Once the move was made the department of Indian affairs broke every promise it ever made to these people about housing, education, health and economic development. When they left it burned their traditional community so there could be no return.
The Gwa'Sala-Nakwaxda'xw sank into 30 years of hell, totally engulfed by social disintegration and social problems. One of the measures of these social problems was the fact that 300 children were apprehended by social services and taken out of that community. Some were adopted as far away as Europe, never to return again.
It is our hope that the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples would meet on the north end of Vancouver Island to hold sessions in the community to inquire into the impact of the policy of the department of Indian affairs concerning forcible amalgamation and forcible relocation of Indian people with no commitment to the promises made.
In the case of the Gwa'Sala-Nakwaxda'xw-

Madam Speaker, in a survey last year my constituents expressed concern about the integrity of our immigration system. The majority supported the need to tighten up immigration laws to filter out those who would abuse our system.
I was one of several members who gave up time in my riding last summer to hear witnesses on Bill C-86, the amendments to the Immigration Act.
We were told by Immigration officials of cases where immigration officers would see a passport sticking out of the pocket of would-be refugee but had no right to seize the document. The power to search, they said, would greatly assist them in their efforts to prevent abuse.

February 26, 1993
We learn from the paper today that already those new powers are having an effect. Since the beginning of the month immigration officials have been able to seize several fake passports and documents, in some cases simply by asking people claiming to have no documents to empty their pockets. In one instance the phoney documents led to an RCMP investigation into a smuggling ring.
Canada is one of the most generous countries in the world when it comes to opening its doors to those who seek to enjoy what it has to offer. We want to continue our tradition of compassion but, to ensure this, officials must have the powers necessary to uphold our immigration system.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired.

Madam Speaker, it was sad to learn this morning of the death of one of Cape Breton's finest sons, Danny Gallivan.
The broadcast voice of the Montreal Canadiens for three decades, Danny Gallivan's high-pitched and unfailingly colourful description of the games transfixed hockey fans around the world.
For more than 22 consecutive years he did not miss a single game because of illness. His great contribution to the sport was recognized in 1982 when he was named to the Hockey Hall of Fame.
On a personal note, I count the Gallivan family among my friends and I want to express to them my deepest sympathies.
Danny Gallivan's Canadiens were undoubtedly the greatest hockey team in the world. Their heroes included Maurice Richard, Doug Harvey, Jean Beliveau, Guy Lafleur, Ken Dryden, and too many others to name here. But to me as a youngster, and even today, the greatest Canadien hero of all was the guy from down the road in Whitney Pier, Danny Gallivan.

Madam Speaker, on February 14,1 had the honour and the privilege as the federal member of Parliament for La Prairie to give nearly 50 people in my riding the commemorative medal for Canada's 125th anniversary on behalf of the Governor General.
More than 650 guests attended this ceremony where I was very pleased to honour and thank publicly these volunteers who have worked for many years to help my constituents in the arts, social affairs, culture and sports.
Such tribute had never been paid to them publicly and, as several of them said to me, this will help them continue to work tirelessly and even more eagerly to help the most disadvantaged and those in greatest need.
Congratulations to every one of them on behalf of all my constituents and in my own name. Any well-organized community needs such volunteers and should thank them in appreciation for their good deeds.
Once again, thanks to all.

Madam Speaker, yesterday's budget estimates brought good news for helicopter makers and spies but bad news for women and children.
Spending on military helicopters has skyrocketed from $4.4 billion to $5.8 billion and Canada's spy agency is richer by almost $12 million. Yet $1 million was cut from women's programs, $5 million was cut from the child care initiatives fund, and billions were lost for child care in dramatically reduced transfer payments to the provinces. The health and welfare branch, which funds family planning and health promotion, was cut by $20 million.
February 26, 1993

Funding to prevent unwanted pregnancies and their costly social and economic consequences began a rapid decline under the Liberals and is continuing under the Tories.
Why are military helicopters and spies more important than the women and children of Canada? This government continues to mouth a commitment to equality but takes our society in exactly the opposite direction.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in Parliament the government introduced legislation to implement the North American free trade agreement. The NAFTA is the culmination of 14 months of negotiations and 6 more months of careful drafting of the text and the legislation.
In Canada the level of interest in the agreement is high. That is why the government strongly supported the all-party hearings which took place on NAFTA in nine cities across Canada and in Ottawa during the past four months. Over 100 presentations have been made.
It is now time to start the debate on the legislation itself. I am confident that informed and serious consideration will confirm NAFTA's rightful place as part of Canada's economic strategy.
The NAFTA is only one component of that strategy. That is why the government continues to press for successful conclusion of the Uruguay round of the GATT. Nothing could send a more powerful signal of economic confidence to all world markets.
I do not claim this agreement will produce economic miracles but it will create opportunities for business and in time contribute to solid job creating economic activity.

Madam Speaker, the subcommittee on poverty is no joke. Child poverty is no joke. The fact that one million Canadian children are the clients of food banks is no joke either.
What is both tragic and laughable is the attempt of some hon. members to change the definition of poverty. It reminds me of a British farce entitled Don't Raise the Bridge, Lower the Water.
The philosophical meanderings of government members will be cold comfort for children on social assistance as well as the children of the working poor.
It clearly is time for the children of Canada to pull up their socks. Their government has just said to them: "You are not poor; you merely think you are poor".
It is interesting that today the justice committee tabled the unanimous report that deals far more sensitively and realistically with the whole question of poverty in this country. Perhaps government members on the justice committee could do some missionary work with their colleagues on the poverty committee.

Madam Speaker, during Question Period yesterday I pointed out that regional development spending in Quebec was slated to go up by $40 million, and I welcomed that, while support for similar programs in Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario and western Canada were being cut by $36 million. The President of the Treasury Board claimed in his response that two programs, the Montreal Development Fund and the Canada-Quebec Industrial Development Agreement, had not been approved in time for the 1992-93 estimates so they were included in the new estimates released yesterday and this accounted for the difference.
