Madam Speaker, I rise in the House today to express my concern and dismay with the decision by the government to proceed with new runways at Pearson International Airport.

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions
I am expressing the concern of my constituents who must live with the constant noise generated by Pearson's traffic. My constituents have been plagued by noise from airport operations for years with no relief or sympathy from the federal government. This latest decision by the government will only make an intolerable situation worse for the residents in my riding.
The government's own federal environmental assessment on expansion at Pearson recommended against taking any action at this time. The report by FEARO said there was lots of time to look at alternatives before building more runways. The government has obviously decided to ignore its own advice.
I charge that this decision is unfair and I urge the government to reconsider its course of action. It is up to the government to make sure that the people who live in the shadow of Pearson do not suffer for it.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of National Defence came to Nova Scotia and stated that CFB Cornwallis would probably be closed. This statement was made without ever having visited the base, without having had time to see if it is cost-effectively carrying out its role for national defence and without ever having looked at the devastating effects such a closure would have on the area.
CFB Cornwallis presently trains and has trained since 1968 all English speaking new recruits for our Armed Forces. No matter what happens to this government, no matter which party is in power, we will need our Armed Forces. To sustain our Armed Forces we need new recruits.
Look at the difficulty this government has in meeting our UN commitments. Where would this government train new recruits? Why would it move this training base and incur massive new expenditures? Why would this minister say what she said without even knowing the facts?
I call on the minister to visit CFB Cornwallis before making statements that not only hurt the people in the area but which financially make no sense.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
At a time when more than 1.6 million Canadians have no jobs, at a time when more than one million children are feeding at food banks, the minister is promoting a helicopter deal with management fees alone of over $1 billion.
Yesterday we learned in the government's own estimates that another $1.4 billion had to be set aside for this deal. Can the minister explain why she is promoting a deal with management fees of over $1 billion when she does not have a penny for children at the food banks in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is an extraordinary question.
There are enormous amounts of government money going from the federal, provincial and municipal governments to aid children in Canada. There is only one level of government responsible for national defence and that is the Government of Canada.
In establishing our priorities and investing in equipment that will protect Canadians in the future, that will enable us to participate in peacekeeping operations to preserve our own sovereignty, the Government of Canada, the Department of National Defence, has long-term plans for serious equipment.
As I have said many times, the equipment necessary for the Department of National Defence is not cheap. That is why when the government makes a decision to engage in a particular procurement policy we work very hard to make sure that procurement has the very best possible benefit for Canadians, not just simply in terms of the service provided by the ultimate equipment, but in the spending of that money.
February 26, 1993

That is why one of the things that is so important about this project is that $3.2 billion of industrial benefits come to Canada, 45,000 person-years of employment.
I was recently at a plant in Winnipeg where $260 million will be spent. Half of the members of that work force are women. This is a growing area of the economy which is important for all Canadians. Therefore-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. minister will have the opportunity to continue.

Madam Speaker, we know that Montreal has 250,000 unemployed people. No more money has been provided for them; it is being cut. On the other hand the minister is promoting a helicopter contract with management fees of over $1 billion. The minister never told us that so much money from Canadian taxpayers would go into the pockets of foreign companies.
How can she justify giving over $2 billion from this contract to multinationals in England and Italy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, $975 million from this project will go to Quebecers, in industries in the province of Quebec. It is important to point out, as I said in English, that this project will provide 45,000 person-years of employment for Canadians-men and women. Furthermore, this project will have industrial benefit, which are of the utmost importance for Canada.
It is an investment in the future of our economy which creates long-term jobs and long-term jobs are the best way to guarantee our children's future. It is not enough to educate Canadians and provide them with social services; they must have the chance to use their skills and education so that industry can employ them in the future. That is what we have supported with this investment.

Madam Speaker, some children in Canada have nothing to eat today but the minister prefers to spend $24 million per helicopter in management fees.

According to the government's own briefing we are talking about a management fee for each helicopter of
Oral Questions
more than $24 million. We are talking about a contingency fund per helicopter of $10 million. We are talking about an amount of money going into foreign multinationals of $36 million per helicopter.
Now that the minister finally understands the outrageous nature of this expense will she cancel the contract?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is the most extraordinary arithmetic I have ever heard because if the management fee for each helicopter is $24 million, and I forget the other fee she referred to as being $10 million, we must be getting the helicopters themselves for free because the search and rescue version is $33 million and the naval version is $44 million. We are obviously getting a serious bargain.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 8,1992, when asked in this House about the total absence of a fair public bidding process on the helicopter deal, the government House leader alleged that Boeing Canada had submitted a bid for search and rescue helicopters in June 1990 and that it had been rejected by the government.
Supply and Services documents state that this is not a bid solicitation but an inquiry for price availability.
I want to ask the Minister of National Defence if she will take the opportunity to correct the record and admit that there was never a proper bidding process for these helicopters.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a matter of fact in dealing with the process, the present helicopters were declared in 1978 by the previous government as not being able to meet the needs.
In 1981 it started looking for new types. In 1985 nine companies were asked to bid on it and in 1986 two companies did bid on it. In 1987 National Defence and the evaluation team picked the EH-101 as being able to meet the needs in Canada.
One of the major reasons for that is that the Boeing helicopter, even if refitted, would not have a de-icing capability. If you want to do search and rescue off Newfoundland and maybe take care of some of the fishermen, you need to have a de-icing capability. Otherwise you are looking for a second-hand, used aircraft and leaving your fishermen to the prey of the weather.

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government's helicopters expenditures will result in millions of dollars for management and contingency fees. Yesterday the estimates stated very clearly that an additional $1.4 billion has been set aside for this deal.
I want to ask the Minister of National Defence to confirm to the people of Canada that over $2 billion of the $5.8 billion contract will be going to E.H. Industries, the parent company, with plants in England and Italy. While the minister is on her feet, would she indicate to the House how many jobs will be created in those two foreign countries?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, since they are asking a matter of contract, I should tell the hon. member we have a world-wide mandate on all EH-lOls, about 10 per cent, which will create jobs for all EH-lOls that are made around the world. There are 45,000 jobs of high-tech nature which will be-
Answer the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. A question was asked and the answer deserves to be heard.

The members of the Liberal Party indicate that they feel there could be more jobs created with the same amount of money. We have experienced their make-work programs that last for 20 weeks and then the people go on unemployment insurance.
What we are creating here is a world-class-
Answer the question.

Obviously they do not want to hear the answer. They are only interested in their own rhetoric. Perhaps they could ask the hon. member for Bonavista, who was the Rear Admiral and Vice Chairman of Maritime Command, and who is one of their members who supports this because I want to tell you, Madam Speaker, none of them know what they are talking about.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister, if
I can get an answer from him, regarding transfer payments.
The minister knows that yesterday it was announced that because of the preliminary estimates from Statistics Canada on population figures that equalization for the small provinces of this country will be cut back. In fact, they will be asked to repay some $600 million over the next few years.
The Government of Quebec has said that it is inappropriate and unacceptable to use preliminary statistics in order to base this call for repayment of equalization payments.
I want to ask the minister the following question: why force the poorest provinces of this country to repay equalization based on preliminary figures? Second, why not use some time this summer to convene a federal-provincial conference on the equalization formula to try to adjust the formula which would help the poorest provinces in this country? Why not do that to help the poorer provinces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to note that today the premier of Saskatchewan has been a little more attentive in his statement and said that what we are offering him is a fairly generous pay-back schedule.
That being said, these transfer payments are established by legislation. We are asking for money back but we are also giving hundreds of millions of dollars to the provinces, not because it is the whim of the Minister of Finance but because these are established programs that have an in-law regulation and it varies with population.
As for the legitimate concern raised by the hon. member, he said that they were based on preliminary estimates. We always do that but I can tell him without any hesitation that should these estimates vary and be made more precise in time, we will gladly make the adjustments.
February 26, 1993

Madam Speaker, the minister and his colleague the minister of defence are anxious to spend billions of dollars on helicopters but will not spend a few dollars helping poor people in the poor provinces of this country. That is not good enough.
We have a debt crisis in this country. There is a debt crisis in Saskatchewan. Its debt has increased in the last 10 years from $3.5 billion to some $15 billion. In light of that emergency situation caused by Conservatives in this country, I want to ask the minister whether or not he will consider emergency assistance to Saskatchewan and to some of the other poorer provinces that need it now.
Why all the money for the minister of defence on helicopters and nothing to the poor provinces to help ordinary people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the rhetoric of the hon. member sounds good but his numbers are wrong.
Let me tell him very briefly what we will be transferring to the provinces this year. On the Established Programs Financing, we will be transferring $21,358 billion. That is an increase of $1.3 million. On equalization to transfer money across the country as the needs arise, we will be spending $8.3 billion. On the Canada Assistance Plan it will be $8 billion. This is an over-all increase of $3.2 billion. We will be transferring to the provinces $37 billion this year. If this is not assistance to the provinces, I do not know what is.

Madam Speaker, a supplementary question to the same minister.
In his first answer the minister said that the cuts are a result of legislation. Of course the minister is right. The cuts made by the Liberals in 1982 and the cuts made by the Conservative government in Established Programs Financing have hurt the poorer provinces of this country.
My province alone receives $280 million less in Established Programs Financing. Given that before this last cutback the province was already cutting funding to hospitals, to universities, to municipalities, to school-
Oral Questions
boards, what does he expect the provinces to do to provide services for their citizens?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just indicated that the federal government was transferring $38 billion to the provinces. That is a vast amount of money. In many instances, the provinces can use these moneys pretty well the way they want.
This is a very generous proposal, a very generous system. Of course we would all like to go beyond this and give them even more money. But I would like the hon. member to tell me where we will get it. Will it be through higher taxes or borrowing more money?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the same minister who asked where we would get the money. It is interesting in looking at the estimates that the cost overrun of the helicopters is $1.4 billion. At the same time, the government is retroactively clawing back close to $1 billion from six poor provinces: $293 million from Manitoba; $246 million from Quebec; $76 million from Nova Scotia.
Why is this government paying for the inefficient poor planning of the minister of defence causing a $1.4 billion overrun by taking the money away from the poorer provinces for their health and education systems which help the poor, the young and the sick?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, words, words. Yesterday when the Leader of the Opposition got up, I was very surprised that a former President of the Treasury Board was not able to understand the meaning of current dollars.
The press release where it was indicated that we were going to proceed with these helicopters was written in current dollars. It means that when tailoring them in over a period of 15 years changes which may occur in the markets must be taken into account. Looking at OECD with our own numbers we have factored that in.
The helicopters have not changed in price. It is just the factor and if there is no inflation there will be no increase. This is not a miscalculation. It is a good calculation. I suppose that is beyond the understanding of the Liberals.

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, the one thing we understand is that $5.8 billion is $5.8 billion too much for these helicopters. The President of the Treasury Board talks about understanding what is going on.
I want an explanation as to why the formula used by this government to justify these clawbacks does not meet the regular standards of Statistics Canada. It will not even publish the formula because it is beyond its margin of error. The same formula was rejected by the U.S. government in 1990 because the margin of error was too high. Yet this government persists in using that formula to take away close to $1 billion for poor provinces.
.(1135)
Considering that the government has already set up a $2.6 billion slush fund to use for election promises, is it not much better and much more moral to take the money and give it to the provinces for their health and education systems? Will the government change this deplorable policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I suppose that the hon. member is referring to the $2.6 billion which is there in reserves and is in every budget. He says it is a slush fund because there is going to be an election. I will tell the hon. member that it is lower than the reserves we had last year.
The hon. member was asking questions a couple of days ago about the national AIDS strategy. We said that the minister will be coming forward and we will be funding it. We cannot fund it from thin air so we set aside reserves.
The member is aware, having been in this House longer than I have, that many times throughout the year there are supplementary estimates where additional spending is announced for programs that have not yet been designed. This is where the money goes. There are no secrets.
* *

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister speaking for the Minister of State (Youth).
Wednesday the minister announced that he would freeze the budgets of our Canada Student Employment Centres, just at a time when students desperately need their help.
Why is the minister, at a time when there are close to
500,000	young students looking for work and thousands of other students looking for jobs, freezing such a vital program?
The cost of one helicopter alone could put thousands of young people back to work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to answer this question on behalf of the Minister of State (Youth).
The member will be very pleased to know with respect to the Challenge '93 job program we have set forth in the estimates that there is going to be an increase of some $5 million for that program for the summer of 1993. This is going to be very beneficial to young people in getting jobs.

Madam Speaker, I wish the minister were here because the minister knows he has frozen the vital program needed by students to help them get back to work.
This minister must be aware that in the past five months alone close to 100,000 young Canadians have been forced out of the work force.
What kind of government places a higher priority on helicopters than its unemployed youth? Will the minister make a commitment in this House today to revoke this outrageous freeze and increase the moneys spent on this very vital program for our young people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very proud of this government's achievements with respect to youth, whether it is the start-up program, the stay-in-school program, the SEED program of people starting their own jobs. The youth centres help young people begin their own jobs. It is a very important project in the area of metro Toronto where $178,000 has been put forth for young people in particular to start new jobs.
I am very, very honoured to be part of a government that has put so much emphasis on youth.
February 26, 1993

Madam Speaker, yesterday in a question to the Minister of Finance I quoted from his economic statement which said: "Funding will be increased for the highly successful research assistance program which provides technology support and financial assistance to businesses". I asked him why the estimates showed no such increase.
Amid great hilarity, the minister of science said: "In the estimates there is an increase of over $14 million for science and technology". That was a deceptive non sequitur.
Today I ask the minister of science once more: why, instead of the promised increase was IRAP in fact cut by $1,333 million? This is the most successful technology program, the most successful job program the government has. Why the cuts instead of the promised increase?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I tell my hon. friend that we were both right yesterday. First of all, S and T funding is going to be up considerably over this year. Out of that we will back-fill the decrease of $1.3 million for IRAP. Therefore, we were both right.
He was right. He read the estimates which said that IRAP's estimates are down. That is right. But the over-all point is the S and T envelope is up and we are going to back-fill the difference for IRAP.
What he is interested in and what the House is interested in is government spending for S and T. That is up substantially.

Madam Speaker, the estimates are conceived to deceive and this minister demonstrates it.
If there is a $14 million increase in the $5 billion science expenditure, will this minister table his numbers that yield that total? Will he tell this House why the promise was made by the minister, reiterated by the previous minister of science and technology, that IRAP will be the core, the real delivery mechanism for the
Oral Questions
government's technology diffusion policy? An increase was promised and it is not there. Why is it not there?
Watch your blood pressure, Howard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just because the member is endangering his blood pressure with his question does not make it a different question. The answer is the same.
The answer is that IRAP spending will be the same or up. This is a very important program. I agree with the hon. member. We are diffusing technology in unprecedented ways through this program. It is a core part of what we are trying to do under S and T and we will continue to do it in a major way.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Yesterday, reporter David Lewis Stein of the Toronto Star captured the feeling of metro residents when he wrote: "For four years the greater metro Toronto area has been sinking into a terrifying economic depression and Mulroney has refused to use the power of the federal government to help us".
While the Prime Minister has decided to leave, nowhere is his legacy of economic failure more real than in metro Toronto. Why has the government so consistently abandoned the metro Toronto economy and when will it show a change of heart?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not accept for a moment any accusation of abandoning metro Toronto. Indeed as I read the business publications in this country, all of which are out of Toronto, they seem to be suggesting a lot of the laws, regulations, tax rules and so on coming out of Queen's Park are having a very adverse effect on investment decisions and so on.
The fundamentals we have put in place and the opportunities presented by FTA and NAFTA are soon going to bring back restored vigour and growth. Toronto again will be leading this nation in growth. We may have to have a provincial election before that, but it will come.

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister and the minister from St. Paul's said that they do not buy the economic malaise. I tell the minister that maybe she should visit the riding from time to time and the Prime Minister should visit Toronto and find out exactly what is going on in that city.
Last week at the metro economic summit the federal government through the minister of trade dumbfounded all participants with a speech devoid of any admission of failure and devoid of any meaningful solution.
When will the government finally recognize that by strengthening and making the metro Toronto economy more vibrant it will also be boosting a very fragile national economy? When will it act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in his opening question, we were not challenging the fact that the Toronto economy at the moment is not as buoyant as it historically has been. We were challenging the accusation by the hon. member that it was a deliberate plan and policy of this government and there is no evidence for that.
Last week the Minister of Transport was there to announce expansion at Pearson airport and of course that follows on the terminal expansion announced a while ago.
However when he was talking about vacuous speeches in Toronto, I think he was referring to the one at the Empire Club a few days ago.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Seniors. In yesterday's estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare the Seniors Independence Program has "made important and positive differences to seniors". Despite this, there is only $3.5 million in funding for this program.
How can the minister justify a 75 per cent cut in this important and positive program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Seniors)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I really do not know where the hon. member got his information.
We met our commitments in the past five years, as we implemented our senior citizens initiative. I agree that New Horizons and the Seniors Independence Program are excellent programs which help retired seniors to remain independent and keep active.
The initiative is drawing to a close, being a five-year project. These issues are on the table, funding renewal is expected, and support for seniors and their initiatives will always be maintained.
I really do not understand your question and I object to giving seniors the impression that we deceived them.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
Yesterday in a letter the Minister of State for Seniors indicated her government was committed to improving the quality of life for seniors.
Considering that the government can find $5.8 billion for Cadillac helicopters and not one red cent for seniors' health issues under the National Health Research and Development Program, how can the minister state that this government is committed to seniors?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Seniors)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just said we have a five-year initiative that expires at the end of March 1993.1 would therefore ask members opposite to be patient, since discussions are going on in Cabinet. At the appropriate time, we will announce certain investments and the renewal of certain initiatives, including the availability of funds for research on geriatic diseases.
As a government we have shown leadership in this area and our record compares well with what has been done internationally if we consider the social and economic measures we have introduced to protect the independence of senior citizens.
February 26, 1993

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence on what must be becoming her favourite subject.
Yesterday's figures show that the $5.8 billion helicopters-that is $116 million per helicopter-make them the most expensive military helicopter in the world.
The minister persists in trying to defend these helicopters on their value as search and rescue helicopters. Was she aware when she approved the purchase of the helicopters that not a single other government in the world is going to use these helicopters for search and rescue purposes? Can she name a single government that is going to make that use of these helicopters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all it is important to point out that the hon. member is quite in error when he talks about the helicopters costing $100 million.
We are talking about a helicopter project, not simply the cost of the hardware. About half of that cost is for the helicopters themselves, a quarter of it is for logistic support and a quarter for contractors and government management costs and contingencies. In other words, the helicopters themselves cost about-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not possible to have helicopters without having logistic support. In other words, it is a project and the figures have always been out front. They have been public. They were published in 1992 dollars and we have budgeted responsibly to make sure that there are no unforeseen overruns and that Canadians do not wind up facing the possibility of additional irresponsible financial policies by not having contingencies taken into account in the budget.
The hon. member is quite wrong in saying that these helicopters will not be used by others for search and rescue. He should also know that in our own province right now-and I say this because the hon. member is from British Columbia-we do not have the capacity to
Oral Questions
provide helicopter search and rescue north of the Dixon Entrance or Hecate Strait. These helicopters will, for the first time, provide adequate service. The Labrador helicopter cannot do it. You could spend a billion dollars on a Labrador and it will never be able to do it. These helicopters are going to save lives in our province.

Madam Speaker, 80 per cent of the people in the minister's own province, the province from which we both come, have the wisdom to be against the purchase of these helicopters.
In yesterday's estimates the government conceded that the cuts in operational funding for the Canadian forces will lead to this state: "This will affect the ability of the Canadian forces to mount and sustain operations".
Why does the government persist in undermining Canadian peacekeeping and operational capacity and at the same time go on this huge spending spree for equipment that is no longer needed as a result of the end of the cold war? Why will the minister not accept the wisdom of the people of her own province and of a wide range of experts?
Why will the minister not consider the alternative which can fund helicopters at less than $1 billion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, supposing for the sake of argument we cancelled this project.
We could upgrade the existing fleet of helicopters, Labradors and Sea Kings, for about $2.5 billion. TTiat is the actual cost. It gives them an extra 10 years of life. Therefore we get an extra 10 years of life on 1950s technology. We do not get increased range because the additional technology will add increased weight to the helicopters.
As I say, you can spend all the money you want on a Labrador but you cannot upgrade it to take off in winds higher than 35 knots. Certainly where I come from there are a lot of winds higher than 35 knots.
After an additional 10 years of life, after you have spent $2.5 billion on the helicopters, you still have to replace them. You still have people flying in 50-year old aeroplanes.

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions
That is why the House committee, of which he was a member, said unanimously in 1990 that the committee recommends that the Sea King helicopters be replaced as planned with the EH-101 and that this be done as soon as possible to avoid costly stop gap measures.

Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of National Defence. Lately the opposition parties have shown a great deal of concern about the helicopter contracts. Perhaps we should talk about those contracts. I would ask the minister to tell us about the costs involved and about the economic spin-offs for Canada's economy and especially for Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the economic spin-offs for the Canadian economy will total $3.2 billion. This amount will be spread among Canada's regions. In Quebec, for instance, $975 million will be spent, especially in the hightech-sector, which is so important for Canada's future. This expenditure is an investment in the future of our industry in addition to providing services to Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. We know the helicopters will cost $3.2 billion in 1992-93 dollars. We also know that Marc Lalonde's Liberal project for scientific research tax credit was supposed to cost $200 million in 1983-84 dollars but ended up costing more than $4 billion in 1984. We also know that fraud was responsible for $1.9 billion of that amount.
Will the minister confirm to the House that today members of the Armed Forces are prepared to risk their lives to protect and rescue us, and to do so without the equipment they need for search and rescue missions in our Canadian provinces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has raised another important point about the helicopters. The search and rescue capability of the new helicopters is so much greater than that of the helicopters we are using today.
The weather conditions under which our helicopters must operate are very demanding: ice, wind and storms. The new helicopters are able to carry out more difficult
manoeuvres. Furthermore, they will be able to operate under those conditions. And last but not least, they will protect the lives of fellow Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. As you well know, the Government of the Northwest Territories runs one of the most comprehensive and progressive programs and services in the aboriginal languages in all of this country.
The proposed 10 per cent funding cuts will have an immediate, negative impact on both aboriginal language programs and the provision of French language services in the Northwest Territories. Without their language, aboriginal people are without a culture and identity.
I want to ask the minister why the government speaks out to the international community in support of the year of indigenous people and here in Canada does everything in its power to diminish their cultural and linguistic rights and existence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister is very aware and shares the concerns of the hon. member. I know that any cuts that have to be implemented will be done in a fair and equitable way.
One of the realities is that we are in very difficult times and we have all had to undergo the same kind of restraints.
What does she expect us to do? Raise taxes or go deeper in debt? We are fully aware of the importance of doing what the hon. member wants. I am sure that the Secretary of State who is away today on government business will be doing all she can to be helpful in her area of responsibility.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Secretary of State. The fact is that taxes have been raised 36 times and the debt is no smaller, so I think that rests with the government.

February 26, 1993

Oral Questions
Any unilateral reduction of the French language budget contradicts the terms outlined in the Canada-NWT co-operation agreement for French and aboriginal languages. Full implementation of services and programs cannot be carried out with 90 per cent of the funding agreed to.
I ask the minister not to renege on the federal responsibility to assist the NWT in implementing the law of Canada's two official languages policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister understands her responsibility very well and will certainly do all she can, as I said, within her area of responsibility to make sure that she can do what the hon. member wants.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. Can the minister explain to this House why there is $5.8 billion available for the purchase of Cadillac military helicopters while at the same time there is a $30 million cut for minority language education, $2 million being cut from literacy and much more that affects Canadians?
Why is this government's priority helicopters as opposed to people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the grants, contributions and subsidies of all departments have been reduced by 10 per cent. We have been particularly careful in making sure that this will be carried out in a fair and equitable fashion. We are very mindful of the need to continue to develop partnerships.
I know the hon. member has a specific interest in literacy, a program which has brought credit to all of us over the last five years. Under the very exceptional leadership of the National Literacy Secretariat we have seen growing partnerships from coast to coast, individuals, communities and associations that have participated in finding new sources of funding, making people far more aware of the debilitation of being illiterate. I know that we will continue to be able to reach out and have that kind of process in place.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the same minister. An amount of $5.8 billion has been budgeted to buy helicopters. You had the choice but you chose helicopters rather than linguistic minorities, our illiterate, our elderly and native people. What are this government's priorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I said, our priorities have always been to develop partnerships. Throughout the country we have found people who want to participate. Next Monday I will participate with Peter Gzowski, who is himself trying to raise millions of dollars for literacy. The ABC Canada program is another example of business men and women who have been fully involved in helping us in this partnership.
The hon. member asks what we want. We want to help people in need of assistance. It is always the same taxpayers, whatever their taxation level, who do not want to pay more tax because their taxation level is already high enough and too much is already being spent. We will have to tighten our belts one way or another.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, whose department and ambassador have magnificently helped many hundreds of Guatemalan refugees to return from Mexico to Guatemala.
However, as the minister knows, an international delegation, including Karen Ridd of the United Church of Canada, is now visiting displaced civilian communities in the jungle of northern Guatemala that the Guatemalan army now is harassing and threatening at a rising rate according to today's information.
Can the minister tell the House what action Canada is taking to persuade President Serrano of Guatemala to ensure the safety of both these displaced Guatemalans and also the international visitors, and can she tell us

February 26, 1993
Oral Questions
whether the Canadian delegation at the United Nations is pressing for item 12 and a rapporteur on Guatemala?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. He has longstandingly been a member who is very sensitive to issues in Guatemala. I should tell him that our embassy has been instructed to determine just at what stage these attacks are.
We have not actually had confirmation of the attacks but of the preparation for attacks. The embassy will continue, as it has in the past, to do what it can to guard human rights in Guatemala. I do not feel I have the full facts at my disposal yet.
I appreciate the hon. member's interest and will get back to him outside the House if I have anything to add.

Madam Speaker, further to the estimates presented by the President of Treasury Board yesterday, the government says that it is taking back some $230 million dollars in transfer payments from Quebec on the basis of population projections.
I ask the President of Treasury Board if he would agree to set up a federal-provincial committee with Quebec to study the data, which does not seem to correspond to those that Quebec has.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to tell the hon. member that we are in constant touch with all the provinces to discuss problems that can arise with transfer payments.
As for the population projection or census to which he refers, I said unequivocally that the census requires us to spend several hundred million dollars and we are doing so.
If we realize that some figures are inaccurate as we work with them and refine them we will correct them, so the provinces do not need to worry.
 * *

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. During the minister's response to my question she quoted a report to the House of Commons from the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs and she seemed to be reading from the report. It seemed to indicate that the committee not only recommended that the Sea King helicopters be replaced but that they be replaced by the EH-101 helicopter.
As the minister would concede, I hope, the report says no such thing. The recommendation reads in its entirety: "The committee recommends the Sea King helicopters be replaced as planned and that this be done as soon as possible to avoid costly stop-gap measures".
I am sure the minister would also concede that the conditions have dramatically changed since this report was tabled in the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would concede no such thing because in reading the report it is very clear that the plan was by this time, which was November 1990, to replace the helicopters with the EH-lOls. In fact a discussion about concerns that might arise in delay of delivery of the Canadian-built EH-lOls says: "Delays in the delivery of Canadian-built EH-lOls may make it necessary to keep the Sea Kings in operation for longer than expected". Then the committee goes on to make the recommendation "as planned refers to replacing them with EH-101s". I am sorry that I cannot concede to the hon. member's point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

There seems to be a very obvious dispute as to facts.

Madam Speaker, I have a duly certified petition to present. It originates from the New Westminster Presbyterian Church in my riding and is directed to the House of Commons.
The incidence of violence against women and children is unacceptable. Too often the abuser is a close friend, partner or spouse. The present social climate is such that many women feel intimidated or afraid to report incidents of assault or abuse. The present social climate is that when many women report incidents of assault or abuse they are victimized instead of helped. Aboriginal, visible minority, immigrant, disabled, lesbian and poor women face additional overwhelming barriers in reporting violence of abuse and receiving help. Women in the family law systems across the country are trying to protect their children and are suffering from maternal custodial victimization.
Therefore the petitioners humbly call upon Parliament to accept legislation designed to eliminate violence against women and children, encourage and support women to report incidents of assault or abuse, provide assistance and support for women and relief and support for women as mothers and children, emphasize the need for abuser rehabilitation, concentrate special effort on the training of police lawyers, court workers and judges, and focus public attention on this very important and long ignored problem.

Madam Speaker, I think you will find the amendments presently before the House have the support of all parties and actually reflect the excellent co-operation that has characterized the passage of Bill C-99 through the legislative process.
The amendments in group one are designed to improve upon the bill by increasing access to credit by Canada's small business sector. This first group includes two substantive and one technical amendment.
The substantive amendments increase the retroactivity of loans and increase the loan loss sharing ratio to 90 per cent. Both these amendments will have the effect of increasing the number of loans under the program and will increase the availability of working capital. Combined with forthcoming regulatory changes which will both restrict the taking of personal security by the banks
Government Orders
and lending institutions and increase the maximum loan to 100 per cent of the value of the asset, these changes greatly enhance the availability of working capital. This initiative responds to the commitment made by the Minister of Finance in his recent economic statement.
On behalf of the government and the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, who is unavoidably away from the House at this particular time on government business, I would particularly like to thank all members for their support of these very important amendments.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few short comments regarding the amendments to Bill C-99.
I agree with my colleague from York-Simcoe that this was an example of a piece of legislation where all parties co-operated and worked together for speedy passage.
I believe these amendments are in fact substantial. One problem for small business today is that Canadian banking institutions tend to be very rough on small business. This amendment that was put forward in committee increases the loan guarantee by the Crown from 85 to 90 per cent. It should give the banking institutions of Canada a lot of comfort when these bank loan officers make loans to small businesses, which is where our greatest hope for new job creation exists.
The other amendment was substantive and one that we on this side of the House totally support. It was something we were worried about in the bill, but the minister and the committee co-operated. It is an example of, when there is co-operation, how quickly things can move through this House.
In the first bill there was a retroactivity date of 90 days. The minister and the committee, capably chaired by my friend from York-Simcoe, increased that retroactivity period to six months. In layman's terms, that would mean a small business person that bought a capital asset during the last six month period. I say today because it will be passed in this House today. Retroactivity starts on Monday if we get Royal Assent from the Senate by Monday. The six-month period means that moneys put out on capital equipment can be refinanced and it then becomes a part of a small business loan. I applaud the government for accepting that amendment. I think it is really going to make a big difference to small business.

Government Orders
The last point that is so important to a small business person is the cap on the amount of the personal guarantee that is required. So often when a small business person tries to start or expand their business the banks want their life insurance policy, home, children or whatever else they may have. Banks have never been too shy in demanding all those personal guarantees.
I consider this third amendment a substantial one also. It limits the amount of personal security that a financial institution can demand. Therefore, we in the Liberal Party of Canada support all these amendments and we hope the bill can move to third reading quickly so it can become law.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of our member for Okanagan-Similkameen- Merritt, I am speaking on this bill this afternoon.
We support the thrust of the bill and the amendments, especially those that limit the ability of the banks to demand unreasonable security from small businesses.
While I have a chance to speak on the amendments I want to point out that the reason this bill and the amendments are necessary is that the banking community has been very reluctant to encourage small businesses. I, and I am sure many MPs in this House, could go through personal example after personal example where instead of being helped, small businesses felt they did not get the funding they should have got and when they got a loan from a bank they felt almost harassed by those same institutions. I heard an example of someone who was actually making his payments and the bank decided it wanted a larger payment and almost forced that person into bankruptcy as a result.
I have noticed that the government through one of these amendments is basically saying that it will not only provide 85 per cent insurance to the banks, but will provide 90 per cent insurance to the banks. So there is almost no risk to the banking institutions under this amendment. That is quite remarkable. We are asking the banks to do what they should be doing as a business and the Government of Canada has to almost completely insure those loans.
Why are we doing that? We are doing it because we want to help small business. We know that. It is really a culmination of the whole banking system. It almost leads us to question why we are using the banks at all for this particular process. Not to argue about nationalizing the banks, but if the Government of Canada is providing almost all, 90 per cent, of the security for any loans that go in arrears or if there is a problem, why do we have to use the banks?
Related to this is my understanding that through regulation the government is also upping the rate that is going to be charged to the lender. It is now going to be not 1.5 per cent above the prime rate but up to 1.75 per cent maximum.
This is a situation where interest rates have gone down for a number of years. Certainly they have been going down since this bill was introduced into the House of Commons. It seems again that the thrust of the government's actions, in this case under regulations, is to aid and abet the banking industry.
Again I have to wonder why we have to do so much work to ensure the banks do their work.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few short comments on this motion.
My colleague from Thunder Bay, who is not here today because his sister passed away as a result of cancer, was very intent on making sure that this amendment was in the bill.
There are tens of thousands of businesses in rural Canada, small real estate firms, as the member for York-Simcoe mentioned, and life insurance businesses that sometimes are run out of the farmhouse or a small little office.
The way the bill was originally drafted, these people were not eligible. It discriminated against them. The original intention of having real estate firms and life insurance firms in there was to basically make sure that the large land developers and the large insurance companies could not use their techniques of shuffling paper around to get access to the loan. The minister and the members of the committee responded to this clause in a very constructive way.
The other point that will come through in the regulations was discussed in committee. It had to do with car dealerships. As members know, under the Small Businesses Loans Act a small business is defined as a business having sales of less than $5 million.
In a car business, it is the actual sale of the cars. You could maybe sell 20 or 30 cars and you would be over the actual amount of the sales of a small business. The regulations are being drafted to make sure that the portion of the transaction that is handled by a finance company is exclusive. It is not included in the gross sales of eligibility.
I believe that this amendment covers not only car dealerships which may fit the $5 million in sales but also the life insurance companies and the real estate firms. Once again I have to say that this was an example where the committee worked together. It worked quickly and it is going to make this a much better bill.
Now we just have to make sure that the 960,000 businesses that are eligible, those that have sales of $5 million or under, go out and test the banking system and make sure it reacts to it.

We did not want to see this being a boondoggle for the land speculators, real estate speculators. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood.

Madam Speaker, I want to begin by saying that I am actually just as excited as the government is today about getting this bill through the House.
I am excited about this bill going through the House today because this represents a tremendous opportunity for the 960,000 businesses in this country whose sales are less than $5 million. Many of them have tremendous difficulty in getting access to bank credit.
What has happened here today is that a law will momentarily be passed which will say to the financial institutions of this country that if small business people come into their bank and ask a loan officer for some credit to expand and grow their business or start a business and if that business plan which they present to the financial institution is right and makes sense then under this act the Government of Canada will guarantee 90 per cent of the loan. It will insure it to 90 per cent.
Businesses with sales of $5 million will have a loan limit of $250,000 at prime plus 1.75 maximum, and it could be less. When I say it could be less I would like to give a specific example of a banking institution that came to our all-day committee meeting on Tbesday. We worked into the night and heard witnesses from 9 a.m. right through. The Bank of Montreal was represented. One of the witnesses, Mr. Ronald G. Rogers, senior executive vice-president, personal and commercial banking, said: "The Bank of Montreal will do better than 1.75 per cent, in fact on loans for small businesses of $100,000 and under, it will be prime less 1 per cent".
If the prime is at 7 per cent-I realize that it is less than that today but let us just use that figure for discussion purposes. If a person has a small business and is only looking for $100,000 or less the Bank of Montreal will use the Small Businesses Loans Act, under which 90 per cent of that loan is guaranteed, and will only charge 6 per cent.
If this is used by the financial institutions of this country I really do believe it will get the economy of this country going again.

February 26, 1993

I have been standing in this House talking about small business and about getting capital for small business. I have asked questions in this House. I have participated in 50 different debates in this House during the last 3 years on behalf of small business. I have been pleading, practically begging this government to focus its energies on the small business sector because that is where the job creation potential is. That is where the greatest hope for new job creation lies in this country.
It is no secret to anyone in this House or anyone in this country that all the major corporations are downsizing, that they are laying off workers. My goodness, I think of a small city like Hamilton where Stelco and Dofasco laid off something like 1,200 people at a shot, or Oshawa where General Motors laid off thousands of people at a shot. Does the House know what that does to the hope and confidence of a community? We can go into a major mall, not just in Hamilton or Oshawa but anywhere in the country, after there has been a major layoff and almost feel the lack of confidence.
We can tell by the number of purchases in clothing stores, pet stores or, in my case, restaurants. On Dan-forth, Queen, Pape and Gerrard Streets in Toronto there are some of the nicest restaurants in all of Canada. Most of the time these restaurants have line-ups, but in the last eight to ten months it has changed. There are 300 restaurants in my riding. There are restaurants in my riding that represent over 40 different countries. There are a large number of Greek restaurants and a very large number of Vietnamese, Chinese, Italian and East Indian restaurants. They provide the largest number of restaurants, but there are restaurants from many different countries, many different cultures and many different communities. Collectively they employ 5,800 people; they are my Stelco, my Bombardier. In the last eight months people can walk into these restaurants and pick what seat they want because there are no line-ups any more. It is awful.
The confidence and the hope in our communities, no matter what part of the country, has been very low. We cannot get the hope or the confidence from the large corporations because they are all downsizing, they are all bureaucracies and they are all restructuring. Where do we get the jobs? We get the jobs from the entrepreneurship of this country.
I do not mean to be disrespectful but this is sort of like a deathbed conversion. The government is finally begin-
Govemment Orders
ning to realize that small business is where the action is because there is no bureaucracy in small business. If a proprietor of a small business decides over a two or three-hour meeting that he or she wants to expand his factory or buy a new piece of machinery to be more competitive then he or she makes the decision in a couple of hours and goes forward.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Call the bank manager.

The hon. member is so right. That person makes the decision about how he or she wants to move but then says: "Now we have to go meet our bank manager".
For the last two years the financial institutions of this country have been so rocked and shocked by the collapse of Campeau, the Reichmanns, Edper, and the list goes on and on and on.
What have they done during that period? They have put out the word: no more lines of credit. Cut those lines back. No more new loans. It has been small business which has received the brunt of that abuse from the major financial institutions of this country.
Now with this piece of legislation when small business people decide on a way of expanding their business or starting another facet of their business they can go happily and proudly to their bank manager. They can say that the Government of Canada just passed a piece of legislation called Bill C-99 and that 90 per cent of the money the bank gives them is guaranteed by the Crown. It is guaranteed by the taxpayers of Canada. That should make one dramatic difference in the attitude of that bank manager.
A few weeks ago I spoke about the responsibility of banks in helping us reignite this economy. I mentioned in those remarks that banking institutions have to be the only business that I know of where the customers are afraid of the person they are doing business with.
In other words, Madam Speaker, if you and I went out to dinner in a restaurant-whenever you come to Toronto you are welcome and I will take you to one of the nicest restaurants in all of Canada-I will tell you what would happen if we went into that restaurant. You should come to my riding some time. Visit your daughter and come into my riding and I will take you out.
What would happen would be that the maitre d'-is that the first time a Speaker has ever been asked out?

February 26, 1993
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I may answer the hon. member on that. If he does not blush neither will I.

Okay.
Madam Speaker, if you went into that restaurant on the Danforth the maitre d' or the person looking after the tables would wait on you hand and foot. That would happen in any business, such as a clothing or furniture store.
If someone goes into a bank the bank manager says: "We are doing you the favour". With this bill we can flip it around because if someone does not get service with the first loan officer that they meet, if they do not feel comfortable or if they do not feel they are being respected then they can walk across the street to another financial institution.
I received this advice to pass on to the small business sector from the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association. Helen Sinclair, the president, came to my riding a few weeks ago to speak to a conference "Women in Business". We appreciated her candor. She said: "If you walk into a bank and if you don't feel that the chemistry is right, if you don't feel you are getting good service from the person operating the bank, walk out. Walk across the street".
We have 50-odd financial institutions in this country and there are over 7,000 branches. We have a great banking structure in this country. The problem has been that the loan officers-not all of them, there are lots of great loan officers-act in a condescending way toward their customers.
I know that there are other members of Parliament that hear this as many times as I do. It does not matter whether we are Conservative or NDP or Liberal, we are all hearing the same complaints when it comes to financial institutions.
With Bill C-99, the small business person in this country can go to their financial institution and say: "I want some help and I would like you to get your Small Businesses Loans Act forms in place since I believe that my business plan qualifies me, because Mr. or Mrs. Bank Manager, 90 per cent of the loan you are going to give me is guaranteed by the Government of Canada".
I think this will make a dramatic difference. There are 960,000-odd businesses in this country whose sales are $5 million or less. Just think if each one of those businesses
hired one person, we would move that unemployment insurance-welfare liability, which combined today is close to $30 billion including interest payments, down to about $8 billion to $10 billion. Overnight we would have productive people, people with their dignity back, people paying taxes again. Just think what that would do to the deficit and ultimately the debt of this country.
I have had some frustration with this piece of legislation. In fact, the Canadian Bankers' Association mentioned the same frustration. In 1986 it brought to the attention of the government amendments that were needed to the Small Businesses Loans Act in order to make it work. 1987, 1988 and 1989 passed and finally in December 1992 the Minister of Finance put it in his budget papers and it is through the House 60 days later.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to rise and speak on Bill C-99, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act.
As my colleague pointed out earlier it is one of those unique opportunities when we on the this side of the House have an opportunity to agree with and support legislation that this government has brought forward. We have to recognize that our small business community is really the life-blood of our social communities throughout Canada. Small businesses are the major engines of growth in our economy. Eighty to ninety per cent of all new jobs created over the last decade have been created by our small business sector.
Over the past 10 years Canada's large corporations, many of them branch plants of U.S. companies, have fared very poorly in terms of job creation. The figures indicate they have not provided one iota of new jobs over the last 10 years. New jobs in Canada over this 10-year period have been created largely from our small business entrepreneurial sector.
Had it not been for our small business communities from Victoria to St. John's and their ability to create jobs and their ability to attempt to continue the stimulation of the economy, the job loss we have experienced as a result of the restructuring that has taken place with the free trade agreement would have been even greater than it has been. Much of the credit has to go to our small business communities in their demonstrated resilience and their ongoing ability to maintain job creation.

I am thinking back to a previous piece of legislation that passed through this House with the implementing legislation to allow the government investment in the Hibernia oil fields. I was quite upset at the time. I pointed out that the government had decided to spend millions of dollars to basically subsidize yet another energy megaproject.
I come from the province of British Columbia. A few years back in the old Bill Bennett administration hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayers' money was spent in trying to develop the infrastructure for the export of north-east coal. That was another energy megaproject.
I said at the time with respect to north-east coal and also with respect to Hibernia that the number of jobs that can be created from such investment is really veiy limited. One has to spend over $1 million of capital investment in projects such as Hibernia and north-east coal to generate one long-term job.
If we take that $1 million of capital investment and, rather than apply it to the megaprojects that past governments have been so willing to endorse, put it into the small business sector we find that 40 to 50 times the number of jobs will be created: long-term jobs, lasting jobs, jobs that provide cash flow in our communities and tax revenues for the government. We find that 40 to 50 times the number of jobs can be created for every $1 million of capital investment in the small business community than can be created with capital investment in our energy megaprojects and our large business sector.

We all know that the 4,000 to 5,000 job loss directly or indirectly attributed to the free trade agreement has been very damaging to Canada's economy, particularly in the central region, in Ontario and Quebec. There was more and more limited time to fish in the face of the most efficient catching machine in the world in any industry, this enormous efficient capacity encouraged and fuelled by the management program, encouraged and fuelled by the licence limitation program, encouraged by the banks and a government that provided guaranteed loans.
All of a sudden it crashed. The resource in down-cycled years was not there. The fishing opportunity became even tighter. At the same time interest rates began to rise dramatically. People could not catch enough fish to make the payments on their boats. Then the cycle began of the banks seizing their vessels and people being driven out of the industry with a vengeance. There are all kinds of cases where the banks simply said: "We want to get rid of this loan. We do not care. It does not matter. We are worried about other aspects of the economy. We are going to yank your fish-boat anyway and put you out of business in order to get it off our books".
To give some credit to the Liberal government there was a policy that once the guaranteed loan had been dealt with, with the banks, that was it. They were not interested in taking their homes. They were not going after people who had co-signed the loans. They said:
Government Orders
"Enough is enough. We have driven you out of the industry and that is it".
At one point there was a suggestion of putting a couple of hundred million dollars into a buy-back program to relieve these entrepreneurs, these fishermen; to get the capacity out of the industry so it simply did not move away from the bankrupt individual into the hands of another fisher who could be a dentist in Tbronto, the way the government set it up; and simply to keep the capacity in the industry. They thought they would just let it bankrupt its way out. They did not go after the homes or the family members who co-signed.
Then we come to the 1980s. The Liberal government decides it has a fiasco and it hires Peter Pearse who says that the way to deal with it is to turn around and manage the fishing industry like they did the forest industry in British Columbia, to turn the whole thing over to 10 big companies, to increase the ability of a small number of people to catch fish and when they deliver the fish to charge a royalty, to get rid of people within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans who are no longer needed to police a small fleet, and to make the fishers pay for the landing and the landing inspection facilities. There is no need for enforcement.
Then we have the situation where these business people have been absolutely shafted by the banks and by the downturn in the economy, the increase in interest rates, the increase in fuel prices, and have been driven out. Along comes Pearse and says: "Let's drive them out even further". So we get a situation in which Pearse wants to model the fishing industry the same way as the B.C. forest industry so that there are a small number of extremely large fishing operators and the marginal ones are gotten rid of.
At that point in time that comes along. In come the Conservatives in 1984 and they say: "Oh, oh. We see quite a big pile of money that we would like to go back and recoup". They reversed the policy. The policy now was to go after those people who they guaranteed loans to the banks for. They hired a chartered accountant firm to go back and figure out how much money there was and how to put this in place. They then told the chartered banks: "You signed a clause in these agreements years ago to go back and shaft these people. We want you to go after the co-signers. We want you to go after their homes, their cars, and their assets, and clean them out even further".

February 26, 1993
Government Orders
That is exactly what they have done. They have revisited these people who have gone through a horrible period of time. They had rebuilt their lives after this catastrophic event which was a combination of government policy, banking, and a misguided approach to things.
All of a sudden these people are visited again, and it is going on today. They are yanking away homes and forcing extreme payments out of people. It has to change. There is a group called the Fishing Redress Committee headed by an individual named Jack Larson on the coast of British Columbia who lost his vessel and virtually lost everything. He is representative of a large number of people to whom this government owes the removal of this harassment a decade later. It went back after assets that they had because of an obscure clause in this thing. It is really a vengeance that has been visited on these people and it should be removed.
The second issue is the whole question of the advisability of the Pearse program. It is continuing. Its objective is to create a small group of bigger and bigger businesses in the fishing industry. It is driving small businesses out. We have a situation in which the government from day one-when the Speaker was the minister of fisheries I remember him campaigning in the riding I represent and saying: "We don't accept Pearse's program. This is the wrong way to go".
Yet this government for nine years has followed it as if it were the Bible. It has wreaked tremendous hardship against people in the fishing industry and the coastal communities of British Columbia. This is a small business sector of entrepreneurs who have been shafted by the banks and this government's policy, and it is continuing.
We now find that the government has involved itself in another policy, the aboriginal fishing strategy. It is interesting. Small business people are involved in this. I know the member has sat in front of a three-day committee and listened to their concerns but there is no response to the concerns.
The minister stood up and said: "Well, what is the NDP point of view on this particular sector that involves fishers?" It is that the Supreme Court has laid down the aboriginal right to fish. You can fish by chaos or you can fish by an agreement. We support an agreement for these individuals in the aboriginal community and the agreement with-
